newsitem.title: CHINA: China demands clarity on Taiwan in U.S.-Japan pact.
newsitem.headline: China demands clarity on Taiwan in U.S.-Japan pact.

text.p: China on Tuesday called on Japan to clarify remarks by its top spokesman that Beijing's arch-rival Taiwan lay within the scope of a planned revamp of the strategic alliance between Tokyo and Washington.

Chinese state media accused Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Seiroku Kajiyama of trying to preserve the gulf between Beijing and Taipei and denounced his comments as an unprecedented interference in China's internal affairs.
"We express serious concern about the remarks...and ask the Japanese government to make a clear-cut clarification," said Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang.
Tokyo should abide by the terms of its commitments under its peace treaty with China, state radio quoted Shen as saying.
Kajiyama said on Tuesday that the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty included the area north of the Philippines, the Korean Peninsula and Taiwan, and that revisions to the alliance would cover the same area.
China suffered hugely from Japanese aggression in the 1930s and 40s and remains highly sensitive to any signs of resurgent military assertiveness among Tokyo policymakers.
The revision now underway by Washington and Tokyo of their 1978 guidelines governing military cooperation has prompted repeated calls for caution from China.

The strategic revamp is expected to give Japan its highest military profile in Asia since World War Two, but Tokyo leaders have appeared to disagree on the extent to which the new rules will allow joint U.S.-Japan action near Taiwan.

Beijing has considered Taiwan a rebel province since defeated Nationalist forces found refuge there at the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949, and has repeatedly threatened to invade the island if it declares formal independence.

Kajiyama's statement that Taiwan would be within the scope of the revision showed the chief cabinet secretary was one of a number of Japanese who did not want Taipei to reunify with the mainland, the Communist Party mouthpiece People's Daily said.

"This is the first time since the establishment of ties between China and Japan that a senior official of the Japanese government has so brazenly expressed an opinion interfering in China's internal affairs," the newspaper said.
"This is a sign that Japan plans to interfere militarily in the Taiwan question," it said.

In a report on the revision of their guidelines announced in June, Tokyo and Washington did not specify a geographical limit to Japanese military cooperation with U.S. forces that could include mine-sweeping and U.N.-sanctioned blockades.

Members of Japan's ruling coalition have taken different positions on the scope of such cooperation, adding further strain to a Sino-Japanese relationship periodically strained by territorial disputes and lingering memories of World War Two.
Chinese media this week denounced Japanese politicians for visiting a controversial Tokyo shrine dedicated to Japan's war dead on the August 18 anniversary of its 1945 defeat.

"The evil spirits of Japanese class-A war criminals started wriggling in the controversial Yasukuni Shrine where the farce of prayers was being performed," the Xinhua news agency said in a commentary.
Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, who in 1996 angered Beijing by visiting the shrine ahead of the anniversary, had already announced he would stay away this year.
Hashimoto is scheduled to visit China in September to bolster a recent improvement in ties between Beijing and Tokyo.
